plan.text: Here is your plan for Mutiara Tea Bar crew day-one training. Your exam is on Sunday 18 October at 9:00. You have 7 study days and 45 minutes a day. So you will learn 7 lessons: Who is a food handler under FHR 2009, Handwashing and hygiene rules you cannot skip, Allergens: what the creamer really contains, Opening and closing the kiosk by the checklist, Menu codes, prices and what each drink contains, Taking an order in Malay and Building a drink to the sticker in under 90 seconds. We cut Booking your MOH food handler course, Answering "is this dairy-free?" and Cooking pearls and brewing tea to spec. Booking your MOH food handler course: Folded into Who is a food handler: the certificate is one line of SOP section 2 and that lesson teaches it. Your reviews are dated backwards from the exam, so the last one lands the day before. Every answer was checked against your own files.

clips.text:
Booking your MOH food handler course.
Regulation 30 of the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009 says a food handler must attend a food handler training course and hold a Certificate of Food Handlers Training from an institution specified by the Director of the Ministry of Health.
Your one-page summary states it plainly: "This summary does not replace MOH food-handler training. Every food handler must still attend a food handler training course recognised by the Ministry of Health Malaysia and get the certificate." That sentence is the whole node.
You already know from Who is a food handler under FHR 2009 that scooping pearls, pouring milk, sealing cups and washing shakers makes you a food handler. This node is about the piece of paper that lets you legally stand behind the bar. The SOP is not the certificate.
The Mutiara Tea Bar SOP folder tells you how this shop makes drinks — the 30-second steep, the pearl rotation, the sealing temperature. It is a fictional example written for training. It is not issued by MOH, it is not recognised by MOH, and no inspector will accept it in place of the certificate.
The SOP and the certificate do different jobs: the SOP keeps your drinks consistent, the certificate keeps the shop legal. What the MOH course actually contains. A recognised food handler course covers four things that the SOP never touches:
Food-borne illness and how it spreads — bacteria, viruses, cross-contamination, the temperature danger zone between 5 °C and 60 °C. Personal hygiene — handwashing technique, fingernails, clothing, what to do when you are sick. Your summary's reg.
33 ("Remove your overall, apron or head cover before going to the toilet") is examined here. Safe food handling and storage — the numbers in your summary: hot food above 60 °C, chilled retail food between -1 °C and 10 °C, frozen food at -18 °C, food 15 cm from the wall and 20 cm above the floor, first-in-first-out rotation.
Premises and equipment hygiene — cleaning, pest control, waste, and the reg. 32 clothing rules (clean light-coloured overall or apron, head cover, footwear, stored in a locker when not in use). Why you cannot skip it. Reg. 30 and reg. 31(1) put the duty on both of you.
You must not work without training, medical examination and vaccination. The owner must not let you work without them, and must keep the records for inspection. Penalties for most food-handler offences under regs. 30, 31 and 33 minus 38 run to a fine of up to RM 10,000 or imprisonment of up to 2 years.
The clothing offence under reg. 32 is up to RM 1,000. That is the number that makes this a day-one task, not a someday task. The certificate is separate from the anti-typhoid injection. The injection is a medical check by a registered medical practitioner; the certificate is a training course.
You need both before your first shift.
Work these six steps in order. Each one produces something the next step needs — the registration needs your ID, the course needs your registration, the certificate needs the course. Skipping ahead means paying twice or turning up to a course you are not booked on.
Confirm you are a food handler and check your employer's record. Before you book anything, confirm the reg. 2 definition applies to you: you are directly involved in preparing food, you come into contact with food or food-contact surfaces, or you handle packaged or unpackaged food or appliances in the premises.
Scooping pearls, pouring milk, sealing cups and washing shakers all qualify. Then ask your supervisor which institution the shop already uses. Mutiara Tea Bar hires every few weeks, so the manager almost certainly has a preferred provider and may already hold a group booking.
Ask for the provider name and the course date in writing — a WhatsApp message is fine. Confirm the provider is recognised by the Director of MOH. Reg. 30 requires the certificate to come from "an institution specified by the Director". A certificate from an unrecognised trainer is not a certificate — it is a receipt.
Ask the provider directly: "Is your food handler course recognised by the Ministry of Health Malaysia, and does your certificate carry the MOH recognition?" Get the answer before you pay. If the shop has no preferred provider, this is the step where you check.
Your one-page summary points you to the Food Safety and Quality Division of MOH as the authority for the current list. Register and pay, and keep the receipt. Register with your full name exactly as it appears on your MyKad, your MyKad number, and a phone number you actually answer.
Most providers run the course in Malay, some in English, some in both — confirm the language before you book if you are not confident in one of them. Pay and keep the receipt. If the shop is covering the fee, ask whether you pay first and claim back, or whether the shop pays the provider directly.
Those are different cash-flow situations and you want to know which one you are in. Attend the course and pass the assessment. A recognised food handler course is typically one day and ends with a short assessment. Attend it in person unless the provider is explicitly approved for online delivery.
Take notes on the four areas the course covers: food-borne illness and cross-contamination, personal hygiene and handwashing, safe food handling and storage temperatures, and premises and equipment hygiene.
The storage numbers from your summary are the ones most likely to be tested: hot food above 60 °C, chilled retail food between -1 °C and 10 °C, frozen food at -18 °C, food 15 cm from the wall and 20 cm above the floor, first-in-first-out rotation. Collect the Certificate of Food Handlers Training.
The certificate is the document reg. 30 requires. Check three things on it before you leave the venue: your name matches your MyKad, the provider's name is on it, and the issue date is visible.
Photograph it and store the photo somewhere you can reach from your phone — you will need to show it to the manager and possibly to an inspector. Give the original to the manager for the shop's records. The owner is required to keep training, medical examination and vaccination records for inspection.
Complete the medical check and anti-typhoid vaccination. The certificate alone does not satisfy reg. 31(1). You also need a medical examination and vaccination by a registered medical practitioner — in practice the anti-typhoid injection.
Book this at a clinic, bring your MyKad, and tell the doctor you are a food handler so the correct vaccination is given and recorded. Hand both records to the manager: the training certificate and the medical/vaccination record. The owner must keep both for inspection, and must not let you work until both are in place.
The shop's SOP folder is the training — once I have read it and signed it, I am trained and I can start work. Reg. 30 requires a Certificate of Food Handlers Training from an institution specified by the Director of the Ministry of Health.
Your one-page summary states it directly: "This summary does not replace MOH food-handler training. Every food handler must still attend a food handler training course recognised by the Ministry of Health Malaysia and get the certificate."
The SOP is a fictional example written for this training; it is not issued by MOH and no inspector will accept it in place of the certificate. The difference predicts this: if you turn up for your first shift with only the signed SOP, the manager cannot legally put you on the bar, because reg.
31(1) also requires the medical examination and vaccination on file.
Reg. 30 requires a Certificate of Food Handlers Training from an institution specified by the Director of the Ministry of Health — the shop SOP is not a substitute. Reg.
31(1) requires a medical examination and vaccination by a registered medical practitioner in addition to the training certificate; in practice this is the anti-typhoid injection. The owner must not let you work without training, medical examination and vaccination, and must keep those records for inspection.
A recognised MOH food handler course covers food-borne illness and cross-contamination, personal hygiene, safe food handling and storage temperatures, and premises and equipment hygiene. Most food-handler offences under regs.
30, 31 and 33 minus 38 carry a fine of up to RM 10,000 or imprisonment of up to 2 years; the reg. 32 clothing offence is up to RM 1,000. The certificate must carry your name as printed on your MyKad, the provider's name and the issue date, or it will not satisfy an inspection.
You are a new Mutiara Tea Bar crew member starting in two weeks. Your manager has told you the shop uses a provider called SafeFood Training Sdn Bhd, which runs a one-day MOH-recognised course in both English and Malay and charges RM 80. The shop reimburses the fee on production of a receipt.
You have not booked anything yet. Produce a single document — a text file, a note on your phone, or a page in your notebook — that a manager could read in two minutes to see that you are ready for your first shift. It must cover the booking sequence, the two separate requirements under regs.
30 and 31(1), and the specific numbers you will be examined on. Constraints: use only the provider named above and the numbers from your one-page FHR 2009 summary. Do not invent a second provider, a different fee, or a different course length.
If you are unsure about a number, write the number from the summary rather than guessing.
It is Thursday. Your first shift at Mutiara Tea Bar is Saturday morning. You have paid RM 80 for an online food handler course, passed the assessment and printed a certificate. You have not had the anti-typhoid injection. You message the manager to confirm Saturday.
No, the classic milk tea contains milk protein.
The fruit teas have no milk in the recipe.
I can make one with clean equipment, without cheese foam or pudding.
We do handle milk on this bar, so I can't promise zero traces.
ALLERGY: milk!
Let me check the allergen board with you before I take your order.
Hi — is the classic milk tea dairy-free? My daughter is allergic to milk.

Answering "is this dairy-free?"
A parent leans over the counter and asks: "Is the classic milk tea dairy-free? My daughter is allergic to milk." You have four seconds. If you say "yes, we use non-dairy creamer", you have just told a parent that a drink containing milk protein is safe for a child with a milk allergy.
Section 9 of your SOP names the reason: the creamer's own label lists sodium caseinate (milk). Sodium caseinate is a milk protein. "Non-dairy" on a creamer tub is a labelling term, not a safety guarantee. Scenario A of your SOP gives the answer you are allowed to give, in this order: Answer the real question first.
"No, the classic milk tea contains milk protein." Name what is safe. "The fruit teas — FT01, FT02, FT03 — have no milk in the recipe." Say what you will do. "I can make one with clean equipment, without cheese foam or pudding." State the limit honestly. "We do handle milk on this bar, so I can't promise zero traces."
Then act. Say "ALLERGY: milk" out loud to the bar, add ALG to the sticker, and follow the allergy steps in section 9. Step 4 is not weakness. Section 9 says you handle milk, egg, soy and oats on one small bar and cannot promise zero traces — so you tell the customer what you did and let them decide.
A parent who hears the limit can choose. A parent who hears "dairy-free" cannot. The two toppings that break a milk-safe order are +PD (egg pudding — egg and milk) and +CF (cheese foam — cream cheese, cream). Both are on the sticker codes in section 8.
If either is on the cup, the drink is not milk-safe, and you say so before taking payment.
"Non-dairy creamer" means the creamer has no dairy in it, so I can tell a milk-allergic customer the classic milk tea is safe. Section 9 states that the creamer's label lists sodium caseinate (milk) among its four ingredients, so the creamer contains milk protein and "non-dairy" is not safe for a milk allergy.
The SOP's Scenario A marks "Yes, we use non-dairy creamer" as the wrong answer and gives the correct one: "No, the classic milk tea contains milk protein."
The difference predicts what happens next — the wrong answer sends a milk-allergic child home with a drink that can cause swollen lips or breathing trouble, while the right answer moves the order to a fruit tea made with clean equipment.
A parent is at the counter with a young daughter. The parent asks whether the classic milk tea is dairy-free because the daughter is allergic to milk. You are the cashier. Talk it through in English — the parent will answer you, ask follow-up questions and decide what to order based on what you say.
A customer orders and the cashier writes the sticker: Read it against section 8 and section 9. The order is a problem. The customer asked for oat milk to avoid milk, but +PD egg pudding contains milk, so the cup is not milk-safe. Section 8 says the cashier must stop and explain before taking payment.
What you say, standing at the counter: "I have to stop you here — the egg pudding you added contains milk, so this drink isn't safe for a milk allergy. I can make the same brown sugar milk tea with oat milk and pearls or grass jelly instead, using clean equipment.
We do handle milk on this bar, so I can't promise zero traces. Would you like me to change the topping?" If the customer keeps +PD anyway, the allergy note comes off the sticker and the drink is made as a normal order — but only after the customer has heard the milk content out loud and chosen it themselves.
Run this at the counter the next time anyone mentions an allergy. It is the same five moves every time, whether the customer is a parent, a colleague or someone reading the allergen board themselves. Stop and listen for the allergy word.
The moment you hear "allergic", "allergy", "dairy", "milk", "lactose" or a parent speaking for a child, stop taking the order. Do not finish typing it. Section 9 says: when a customer mentions any allergy, the cashier says it out loud to the bar and adds ALG to the sticker. Answer the actual question, not the label.
For the classic milk tea, the answer is: "No, the classic milk tea contains milk protein." Never answer with "we use non-dairy creamer" — section 9 states the creamer's label lists sodium caseinate (milk) and that non-dairy is not safe for a milk allergy. Name a safe alternative by code.
Say: "The fruit teas — FT01, FT02, FT03 — have no milk in the recipe. I can make one with clean equipment, without cheese foam or pudding." Section 8 lists FT02 Lychee Oolong Tea and FT03 Lemon Black Tea as no milk in recipe; FT01 is the third fruit tea on the same list.
Name the drink, not just the category, so the customer has something to say yes to. State the trace limit and let them decide. Say: "We do handle milk on this bar, so I can't promise zero traces."
Section 9 is explicit — you handle milk, egg, soy and oats on one small bar, so you tell the customer what you did and let them decide. Then wait. Do not fill the silence. Call it to the bar and mark the sticker. Say "ALLERGY: milk" out loud, loud enough to be heard over the blenders, and add ALG to the sticker.
Then make the drink the section 9 way: wash hands, new gloves, a shaker and scoop from the clean rack, fresh ice with the clean scoop, no cheese foam or pudding.
Think of the last time a customer asked you a question about a drink and you answered without checking. What would you have said if that question had been "is this dairy-free?" — and which line from the SOP would have changed your answer?

Who is a food handler under FHR 2009.
The SOP folder tells you how Mutiara makes drinks. It does not tell you who the law counts as a food handler, or what you must have done before your first shift. Those come from the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009, P.U.(A) 95/2009, made under the Food Act 1983.
Regulation 2 defines a food handler as anyone who is directly involved in preparing food, comes into contact with food or food-contact surfaces, or handles packaged or unpackaged food or appliances in food premises.
Your one-page summary puts it plainly: crew who scoop pearls, pour milk, seal cups or wash shakers are food handlers. That is the whole bar team, including whoever is on the sealer and whoever is at the sink. The word doing the work is contact. You do not have to cook anything to be covered.
Touching a shaker, a sealing head, a scoop or a cup rim is contact with a food-contact surface. Handling a sealed cup or a bag of dry pearls is handling packaged or unpackaged food. The definition is about what you touch, not about your job title. Once you are a food handler, regs.
30 and 31(1) attach duties before your first shift. You attend food handler training and get a Certificate of Food Handlers Training from an institution specified by the Director, MOH-recognised. You go for a medical check and vaccination by a registered medical practitioner — in practice, the anti-typhoid injection.
The owner must not let you work without training, medical examination and vaccination, and must keep those records for inspection. Reg. 31(2) covers illness: if you have, carry, or may have a food-borne disease, do not enter the food premises or handle food, report it to management immediately, and stay off work until a registered medical practitioner certifies you cured and fit to work.
The penalties are real. Most food-handler offences under regs. 30, 31 and 33 minus 38 carry a fine of up to RM 10,000 or imprisonment of up to 2 years. The clothing offence under reg. 32 carries a fine of up to RM 1,000.
The summary is not legal advice and the regulations may have been amended since 2009 — check the current text with the Food Safety and Quality Division, MOH.
Role A — pearl station. You scoop cooked pearls from the warmer into cups. You are directly involved in preparing food and you contact the pearls and the scoop. Food handler under reg. 2. Reg. 30 and 31(1) apply before your first shift. Role B — sealer and cup runner.
You take the filled cup, wipe the rim and run the sealer. You never touch the drink itself, but you contact the cup rim and the sealing head — both food-contact surfaces — and you handle the packaged cup. Food handler under reg. 2. Same duties. Role C — shaker wash-up. You rinse and sanitise shakers between orders.
You contact a food-contact surface. Food handler under reg. 2. Same duties. Role D — cashier. You take payment and hand over the sealed cup. Handing over a sealed cup is handling packaged food, and the cashier also answers allergen questions and prints the sticker. Food handler under reg. 2.
Same duties — the summary's definition includes anyone who handles packaged or unpackaged food in food premises. What the four cases have in common: the test is contact, not cooking. If the answer to "do I touch food or something food touches?" is yes, regs. 30 and 31(1) apply to you.
The SOP folder is the only rule that applies behind the bar — if I follow the SOP, I am compliant. The SOP is the shop's operating procedure. The Food Hygiene Regulations 2009 sit above it as law, and they impose duties the SOP may not repeat — reg. 30 training and the Certificate of Food Handlers Training, reg.
31(1) medical examination and vaccination, reg. 31(2) staying off work when ill, reg. 32 clothing, reg. 33 personal hygiene. The difference it predicts: a shop with a perfect SOP and an untrained, unvaccinated crew member is still in breach, and most food-handler offences carry a fine of up to RM 10,000 or imprisonment up to 2 years.
Reg. 2 defines a food handler by contact: preparing food, touching food or food-contact surfaces, or handling packaged or unpackaged food or appliances in food premises. Scooping pearls, pouring milk, sealing cups and washing shakers all fall inside the reg. 2 definition — the whole bar team, not just whoever cooks.
Reg. 30 requires food handler training and a Certificate of Food Handlers Training from an institution specified by the Director. Reg. 31(1) requires medical examination and vaccination by a registered medical practitioner, and the owner must not let you work without all three and must keep the records. Reg.
31(2) requires you to stay out of the premises and report immediately if you have, carry, or may have a food-borne disease, until a registered medical practitioner certifies you fit. Most food-handler offences under regs. 30, 31 and 33 minus 38 carry a fine up to RM 10,000 or imprisonment up to 2 years; the reg.
32 clothing offence carries a fine up to RM 1,000.

Handwashing and hygiene rules you cannot skip.
Two hand-washing failures are invisible on a clean-looking bar: washing too briefly, and not going to the sink at the moment you were supposed to. The law sets the moments; the SOP sets the time. Section 10 of the Mutiara SOP splits every hygiene rule into two columns: [LAW] and [SHOP].
The source column is not decoration. A [LAW] rule comes from Malaysia's Food Hygiene Regulations 2009 (FHR 2009) and carries a regulation number — reg. 33(1)(c), reg. 36(1)(e). A [SHOP] rule is ours. Break a [SHOP] rule and the shift lead corrects you. Break a [LAW] rule and the shop is exposed, not just you.
The hand rule itself is reg. 33(1)(c): wash hands before starting work, right after using the toilet, and after handling raw food, rubbish or anything dirty. Our house rule adds three more triggers: money, your phone, your face.
Twenty seconds is the number: the opening checklist says wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds. Not "until it feels clean" — count it. Soap, running water, backs of hands, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, wrists. Twenty seconds is roughly singing "Happy Birthday" twice through at normal speed.
Two rules sit next to the sink and are easy to skip. Take off your apron and cap before you go to the toilet (reg. 33(1)(b)) — the apron is what touches the drinks, and it does not go into the toilet with you.
And cover any cut with a blue waterproof plaster, then a glove over it; blue because nothing in a milk tea is blue, so a lost plaster is visible in the cup.
Twenty seconds is just a guideline — if my hands look clean and I used soap, I'm fine. Reg. 33(1)(c) requires the wash, and the SOP's opening checklist sets the standard for it: soap for at least 20 seconds. A five-second rinse fails that standard regardless of how the hands look.
What twenty seconds buys you is the scrubbing of the areas a quick rinse never reaches: between fingers, thumbs, wrists and under the nails, where the residue that transfers into a drink actually sits.
The difference predicts what reaches the cup: a five-second wash leaves what was on your hands, a counted twenty seconds removes it.
This is the wash you perform at the sink behind the bar. Twenty seconds, counted, every time one of the triggers fires. Wet your hands and forearms under running water. Turn the tap on and let the water run over your hands and up past your wrists.
Do not fill the basin and dip — running water carries residue away, standing water holds it. Apply soap and start the count. One pump of liquid soap into your palm. Start counting twenty seconds now, not after you have finished lathering. Roughly two slow rounds of "Happy Birthday" at normal singing speed.
Scrub palms, backs of hands and between fingers. Rub palm to palm, then the back of each hand with the other palm, then interlace your fingers and work the soap between them. This is where the residue from money and phones sits. Scrub thumbs, fingertips and wrists. Rotate each thumb inside the opposite palm.
Rub your fingertips into your palms to work under the nails. Finish with each wrist. Rinse under running water. Rinse from wrists down to fingertips so the soap and the residue travel off your hands, not back up your arms. Dry with a paper towel and use it to turn off the tap.
Dry your hands fully on a paper towel, then use that same towel to grip the tap handle and turn it off. Bin the towel.
It is 7:40 pm on a Friday. The queue is eight deep, you are the only one on the bar, and the brown sugar milk teas are backed up. You just took a fifty-ringgit note from the customer in front of you and handed back change. The next order is a BS01 and the pearls are already scooped into the cup.

Allergens: what the creamer really contains.
A milk allergy is not a preference: section 9 lists trouble breathing among the reactions. Your creamer label is the single most dangerous object on the bar, because it says non-dairy and contains milk. Section 9 of the Mutiara SOP lists the four ingredients on the creamer label:
"Non-dairy" on the tub is not a promise that the creamer is free of milk. This one contains sodium caseinate, so it is unsafe for a milk allergy. The SOP states it flatly: "Non-dairy creamer" is NOT safe for a milk allergy. It contains milk protein. Never tell a customer that non-dairy means dairy-free.
On this bar you also handle egg, soy and oats. Section 9 tells you to be honest about that: you cannot promise zero traces, so you tell the customer what you did and let them decide.
If someone reacts — swollen lips or face, trouble breathing, hives, vomiting — you call 999 at once, tell the shift lead, keep the person still, and ask whether they carry their own adrenaline auto-injector. You give them nothing to eat or drink.
"Non-dairy creamer" means there is no milk in it, so classic milk tea is safe for a milk allergy. The creamer label lists sodium caseinate (milk) as its third ingredient. Sodium caseinate is a milk protein, so a creamer sold as non-dairy can still be unsafe for a milk allergy.
The SOP's own wording is that you must never tell a customer that non-dairy means dairy-free.
It is 18:40, the queue is eight deep, and you are alone on the POS while the bar works through a rush. A parent leans in and asks: "Is the classic milk tea dairy-free? My daughter is allergic to milk." The bar is loud, the shift lead is at the back restocking cups, and the parent is waiting for a yes or a no.
The creamer label lists four ingredients: glucose syrup, vegetable oil, sodium caseinate (milk), and emulsifier (soy lecithin). Sodium caseinate is a milk protein, so "non-dairy creamer" is not safe for a milk allergy and you must never say that non-dairy means dairy-free.
The classic milk tea contains milk protein; the fruit teas FT01, FT02 and FT03 have no milk in the recipe. Every tea-based drink on the board carries caffeine; the brown sugar syrup and the toppings do not.
A declared allergy is spoken out loud to the bar as "ALLERGY: milk" and marked ALG on the sticker before the drink is built. An allergy order is built with washed hands, new gloves, clean-rack shaker and scoop, fresh ice with the clean scoop, and no cheese foam or pudding.
We handle milk, egg, soy and oats on one small bar, so you tell the customer what you did and let them decide rather than promising zero traces.
Think of the busiest minute you have seen on a bar. In that minute, which single step of the allergy order is most likely to be skipped — the spoken call-out, the ALG sticker, the clean scoop, or the trace warning — and what would you personally do to make sure it is the one step you never skip?

Opening and closing the kiosk by the checklist.
A kiosk that opens late loses the 10:00 rush. A kiosk that closes sloppy carries cooked pearls into tomorrow, and the SOP is clear that cooked pearls are made fresh every day and thrown away at close. Your SOP splits the day into two checklists. Section 3 of the SOP sets the shifts:
The opening shift arrives at 09:30 with thirty minutes before the doors open. That half hour is not slack: it holds the handwash, the uniform, the chiller and freezer readings, the date labels, the first batch of pearls (about 50 minutes), the tea, the ice, sanitising and the sealer test.
Skip one and you either open late or open with equipment that has not been verified. The closing shift arrives at 15:50 and finishes at 22:30. The shop closes at 22:00, but the closing checklist runs from 21:30 to 22:30 because the last hour is where the cut-offs live: stop cooking new pearls at 21:30, last orders at 21:55, and every cooked pearl in the pot goes in the bin before you lock up.
The SOP is explicit that cooked pearls, brewed tea and opened fresh milk and oat milk are prepared fresh every day — they are discarded, not stored. Two failures the checklists exist to prevent: a bar opened without anyone washing their hands, and pearls carried into the next day. Both are invisible at the time.
The opening checklist is section 4 of the SOP, run from 09:30 so the kiosk opens at 10:00. Each step below is one bullet of section 4, in the SOP's order, with the [LAW] or [SHOP] tag the SOP prints beside it. Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds. Do this before touching anything behind the bar. [LAW, reg.
33(1)(c)]. Put on the uniform and take off jewellery. Shop T-shirt, light-coloured apron, cap, closed shoes. Remove rings, watches, bracelets and pins. [LAW, regs. 32 and 33(1)(f)]. Read the chiller and freezer thermometers and log both. Write both readings in the temperature log.
The chiller must be 4 °C or below, the freezer -18 °C or below. If the chiller is above 5 °C, tell the shift lead before using any milk. [SHOP]. Check date labels. Throw away anything past its use-by time and record it in the waste log. Use stock first in, first out. [LAW, reg. 38(1)(i)].
Start the first batch of pearls. Follow section 6.1. A batch takes about 50 minutes, so start it first, before the tea. Brew the teas and check the syrup. Brew black tea and jasmine green tea (section 6.2). Check the brown sugar syrup; make more if the bottle is under half full (section 6.3).
Fill the ice bin with the ice scoop. Never scoop ice with a cup or your hands. Leave the scoop in its holder, handle up. [SHOP; ice must be protected from contamination, LAW reg. 35(1)(j)]. Sanitise the counter and equipment. Sanitise the counter, shakers, jugs and the sealing machine plate.
Load the cup film and test the sealer. Load the cup film and test the sealing machine on an empty cup. Set up the counter and open at 10:00. Turn on the POS, check the RM 200 float in the cash drawer, put out the DuitNow QR stand, the menu and the allergen board. Open at 10:00.
If I stop cooking pearls at 21:30 but there are still pearls in the pot at 22:00, I can leave them for the opening shift to use first thing tomorrow. The SOP states that cooked pearls, brewed tea and opened fresh milk and oat milk are prepared fresh every day and are discarded at close.
There is no keep-for-tomorrow option, however good they look; section 6.1 already limits cooked pearls to 4 hours in the warmer. The waste log exists so that over-cooking shows up as a number the manager can act on, instead of as a pot someone quietly keeps.
You have read both checklists. Now run them. Scenario. You are on the opening shift on a Tuesday and the closing shift on the same day. A shift lead watches both and signs off. Constraints. Opening: arrive by 09:30, doors open at 10:00.
You may not skip a step to make the time — if you are behind, the shift lead decides what to cut, not you. Closing: the 21:30 pearl cut-off and the 21:55 last-orders cut-off are hard. You may not serve a drink after 21:55 and you may not start a pearl batch after 21:30.
Every discard goes in the waste log with an amount, including anything you throw away because you were unsure whether it was opened today. The photo of the completed closing checklist goes in the crew group chat before you lock up (section 5). Done looks like.
Two completed checklists, both photographed and posted, with no step marked done that you did not actually do, and a waste log entry for every discard.
Think about the last hour of a shift you have worked or watched. Which single step in the closing checklist is the one most likely to be skipped when the shop is busy, and what would you change about the way the checklist is run so that it is not skipped?

Menu codes, prices and what each drink contains.
A sticker reads BS01-L 50% LI OAT +PD ALG:milk. You have four seconds to turn that into a drink, a price and a warning. The price is not RM 10.90 — large is RM 12.90. The syrup is not fructose — BS01 uses brown sugar syrup.
And ALG:milk plus +PD is a stop: egg pudding contains milk, so the cashier stops and explains before taking payment. Section 8 of the SOP lists nine drinks. Learn the code, the two prices and the contains line as one unit: Two families split the syrup. Brown sugar drinks — BS01 and BS02 — use brown sugar syrup.
Every other drink uses fructose syrup. The pump counts are identical either way, so the only thing that changes is which bottle you reach for. Section 7 sets one pump at 10 ml: regular 100% is 4 pumps, large 100% is 6 pumps.
Large is not a fixed number of pumps more than regular: 100% is 4 and 6, 75% is 3 and 5, 50% is 2 and 3, 25% is 1 and 2, 0% is 0 and 0. Read the row. Ice has its own sticker codes: NI, LI, RI, HOT. Regular normal ice is one 120 g scoop; large normal ice is 1.5 scoops, 170 g.
HOT exists only for CT01, CT02 and MT01, regular size only.
Split the sticker into its six fields. BS01 — Brown Sugar Milk Tea with Pearls. Brown sugar family, so the syrup is brown sugar syrup, not fructose. -L — large, 700 ml. Price is RM 12.90, not RM 10.90. 50% — 2 pumps regular, 3 pumps large. Large, so 3 pumps, 30 ml. LI — less ice.
Large, so 1 scoop, 85 g (half a scoop, 60 g, is the regular size). OAT — swap to oat milk, +RM 2.00. This is a gluten flag: the SOP says the oat milk is not certified gluten-free. +PD — egg pudding, +RM 2.00. Contains egg and milk. Price if it were servable: RM 12.90 + RM 2.00 + RM 2.00 = RM 16.90.
But ALG:milk is on the sticker. The customer has a milk allergy. OAT replaces the fresh milk, but +PD contains milk, so the drink as written is not safe. Section 8 of the SOP is explicit: the cashier must stop and explain before taking payment. You do not make this drink.
You explain, offer a drink with no milk in the recipe (FT01, FT02 or FT03) without cheese foam or pudding, follow the allergy steps in section 9, and let the customer choose.
A large cup is just more of the same drink, so I charge the regular price and use the regular pump count. Section 8 lists two prices per code: BS01 is RM 10.90 regular and RM 12.90 large. Section 7 lists two pump counts per sweetness level: 100% is 4 pumps regular and 6 pumps large.
Charging RM 10.90 for a 700 ml cup undercharges by RM 2.00, and using 4 pumps in a large cup makes the drink weak. The size letter on the sticker decides both the price and the pump count.
Which of the nine codes do you still have to look up rather than recall, and what will you do on your next shift to close that gap before the customer is standing in front of you?
Teh susu kurang manis, kurang ais, satu.

Building a drink to the sticker in under 90 seconds.
At Mutiara Tea Bar, a drink is not built from memory. It is built from the sticker. Section 6.4 of your SOP opens with the rule that decides everything after it: read the sticker first. The sticker carries five things you must transfer into the cup — size, sweetness, ice, milk type, toppings.
Miss one and the drink is a remake. The most serious miss is milk type. If the sticker says OAT and you pour fresh milk, an allergy customer drinks dairy. Section 6.4 step 1 puts that in plain words: wrong milk for an allergy customer is the most serious mistake in this shop. The second rule is order.
Syrup goes in before ice. Ice before syrup washes the stripes off the cup wall and you cannot get them back. Brown sugar drinks are never shaken at the bar — the customer shakes, after they leave. The target is under 90 seconds per drink. That is not a speed contest; it is a rhythm.
Read, scoop, stripe, ice, milk, tea, seal, hand over. Each step has one thing that goes wrong, and the SOP names it next to the step so you can catch it in the second it happens. Your cup sizes are fixed: 500 ml regular and 700 ml large. Your milk volumes are fixed: 160 ml regular, 220 ml large.
Tea: 100 ml regular, 140 ml large. Pearls: 1 scoop (60 g) regular, 1.5 scoops (90 g) large. Only the size letter changes these numbers; sweetness, ice and milk type come from the rest of the sticker.
This is BS01 Brown Sugar Milk Tea, built to a sticker that reads: BS01-L 75% LI OAT. Large cup, 75% sweetness, less ice, oat milk. Follow the eight steps in this order. The order is forced — syrup before ice, milk before tea — and reversing any pair changes the drink. Read the sticker out loud.
Say the five fields to yourself before you touch anything: size (R or L), sweetness (%), ice level, milk type (fresh or OAT), toppings. Scan for ALG. For BS01-L 75% LI OAT you say: large, 75%, less ice, oat, pearls. Scoop the pearls. Use the slotted pearl spoon. Large cup: 1.5 scoops = 90 g.
Regular cup: 1 scoop = 60 g. Drop them into the cup first. Stripe the cup with warm syrup. Take the brown sugar syrup bottle from the warm water bath on the bar (or refill it if empty). Add the syrup for 75% sweetness: section 7 gives 5 pumps (50 ml) for a large cup, 3 for a regular.
Tilt the cup and turn it so the syrup coats the inside wall — that is the tiger stripe. Add ice for the sticker's ice level. Use the ice scoop. LI means less ice: 1 scoop (85 g) in a large cup, half a scoop (60 g) in a regular one (section 7). Drop ice in after the syrup. Pour the milk slowly over the ice.
Large cup: 220 ml. Regular cup: 160 ml. This sticker says OAT, so pour oat milk — not fresh. Pour slowly, over the ice, not down the side. Top with black tea over the back of a spoon. Large cup: 140 ml. Regular cup: 100 ml. Pour slowly over the back of a spoon so the tea floats as a layer on top of the milk.
Wipe the rim, seal, and invert over the sink. Wipe the cup rim dry with a clean cloth. Seal with one full press of the handle. Turn the cup upside down over the sink for 2 seconds. Stick the sticker on and hand over. Press the sticker onto the cup. Give a 12 mm wide straw — a thin straw blocks on the pearls.
Read the order number aloud, then say the sweetness and milk type: "Large brown sugar, 75 percent, oat milk." Tell the customer: shake before drinking.
Sticker A: BS01-R 50% RI — regular, 50% sweetness, normal ice, fresh milk. Pearls: 1 scoop = 60 g. Syrup: 50% = 2 pumps, from the warm bath, tilted to coat. Ice: RI = 1 scoop (120 g), after syrup. Milk: 160 ml fresh, poured slowly over the ice. Tea: 100 ml black, over the back of a spoon.
Seal, invert 2 s, sticker on, 12 mm straw, order number read aloud. Sticker B: BS01-L 75% LI OAT — large, 75% sweetness, less ice, oat milk. Pearls: 1.5 scoops = 90 g. Syrup: 75% = 5 pumps, warm, tilted to coat. Ice: LI = 1 scoop (85 g), after syrup. Milk: 220 ml oat, poured slowly over the ice.
Tea: 140 ml black, over the back of a spoon. Seal, invert 2 s, sticker on, 12 mm straw, order number read aloud. The steps are identical. The values change: pearl scoops, pumps, ice, milk volume and type, and tea volume. Everything else — the order, the tilt, the slow pour, the seal — is the same on both.
That is why the 90-second target is reachable: you are not learning two drinks, you are reading two stickers.
The stripes are decoration. If I'm rushing, I can skip the tilt-and-turn and just pour the syrup straight in. The stripes are the product. Section 6.4 step 3 exists because warm syrup coating the cup wall is what makes this drink BS01 and not a plain milk tea with syrup stirred in.
The SOP also tells the customer to shake before drinking — the shake is what mixes the stripes into the drink. If you skip the stripe, there is nothing to shake and the customer gets a flat brown cup. The 90 seconds is a rhythm, not a reason to drop a step.
It is 7:40 pm, the queue is six deep, and you have three stickers on the rail. The third one reads BS01-L 75% LI OAT. You reach for the syrup bottle on the shelf because the warm bath bottle is empty and you do not want to refill it mid-rush.
Your shop is about to train two new crew next week. You are writing the one-page card that will sit taped to the BS01 station — the thing a new crew member reads while their hands are moving. The card must cover the build for both cup sizes and all three milk/ice variants the sticker can carry.
Use these stickers as your test set: BS01-R 50% RI. BS01-L 75% LI OAT. BS01-R 100% NI. Constraints: One page. A crew member must be able to read it in under 30 seconds while a drink is on the counter. Every step must carry its own warning — what goes wrong if that step is done late, done cold, or skipped.
Every number must come from the SOP: cup sizes, pearl weights, milk volumes, tea volumes, straw width, invert time. No prose paragraphs. Tables, numbered steps and short warnings only.
Done looks like: a card a crew member who has never built a BS01 can follow, top to bottom, without asking you a question, and produce a cup that passes the sticker check.

Taking an order in Malay.
A customer steps up and says six words. You catch teh susu and reach for the sticker. If that is all you caught, you will write CT01-R 100% RI — and the customer will send it back, because they said kurang manis and kurang ais. Section 7 of your SOP gives the mapping.
The customer's words and the sticker code are two different languages, and your job is the translation: "Teh susu kurang manis, kurang ais, satu" is one milk tea, less sweet, less ice: CT01-R 50% LI. Three facts, three parts of the sticker. Satu is the quantity — one cup. It never changes the recipe.
Ice works the same way: kurang ais is LI, tak nak ais is NI, ais biasa is RI, panas is HOT. Section 7 also sets the floor on brown sugar drinks: BS01 and BS02 cannot go below 25% because the syrup is what makes the stripes. If a customer asks for 0% on a BS drink, offer 25% or a CT01 at 0% with pearls.
One more word decides where the cup goes. Bungkus — or tapau — means takeaway. Minum sini means drinking here. Same drink, same sticker, different bag.
Order 1. "Teh susu kurang manis, kurang ais, satu." teh susu to CT01, regular. kurang manis to 50%. kurang ais to LI. satu to one cup. Sticker: CT01-R 50% LI. Order 2. "BS01 besar, sikit manis, bungkus." BS01 to Brown Sugar Milk Tea. besar to L (large). sikit manis to 25%. bungkus to takeaway.
Sticker: BS01-L 25% RI — ice is normal because nothing was said about it. Order 3. "Teh susu, tak nak gula, kosong." teh susu to CT01, regular. tak nak gula / kosong to 0%. Sticker: CT01-R 0% RI. This one is fine — CT01 is not a brown sugar drink, so 0% is allowed.
The same request on a BS01 gets the section 7 offer instead: 25%, or a CT01 at 0% with pearls.
A customer walks up to the counter and orders in Malay. You are the crew member on the register. You must understand the order, confirm it back, and write the correct sticker.
